strengths: The paper proposes two intuitive, lightweight additions to GRPO: response-level KL weighting (RER) and periodic validation-anchored policy resets (VAPR). Treating this as an Algorithms/General contribution is appropriate.
The three-stage pipeline is clearly described, and the manuscript provides useful pseudocode, prompts, hyperparameters, computational-overhead measurements, and model-size/group-size studies.

Results are competitive across two established datasets and multiple linguistic and clinical metrics. The same-backbone ablation shows consistent improvements from RER and VAPR over constant-KL and no-reset variants.
The supplementary reward analysis is valuable: it examines reward variance, exposes potential RadGraph reward hacking, and compares BLEU-4 and RadGraph rewards empirically.

The presentation is generally clear, with informative figures and extensive supplementary material. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/204d5e8fdad4459eb8debea8dc3cb84f/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The empirical case lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, or significance tests. The method-level improvements over constant KL are modest (e.g., BLEU-4 0.138 to 0.143 and CheXpert F1 0.484 to 0.506), so it is unclear whether they are robust to seeds, the randomly selected 10k-example RL subset, or checkpoint selection.

VAPR combines two interventions: resetting the reference and rolling the current/old policies back to the validation-best checkpoint. The ablation does not separate these effects or compare against periodic early-stopping rollback, reference-only updates, or EMA. Consequently, the evidence does not establish that clearing accumulated KL pressure—rather than ordinary rollback—is responsible for the gain.

VAPR repeatedly uses the validation set during optimization and selects a checkpoint with a composite validation score. This risks adaptive validation overfitting, particularly on small IU-Xray, yet no held-out model-selection set, sensitivity analysis, or repeated-split experiment is provided.

The claimed clinical superiority is insufficiently supported. Evaluation relies entirely on automatic CheXpert and RadGraph agreement with reference reports, without radiologist assessment, factual-error analysis, calibration, or external-dataset validation. Moreover, the classifier prompts are trained from CheXpert-derived labels, making improvement on CheXpert-based evaluation partly metric-aligned. Claims of superior clinical factual consistency should therefore be tempered.

Several technical details are incomplete or inconsistent: Eq. (2) is undefined when all four rewards have zero variance, and Eq. (8) is undefined when group entropies are equal, with no epsilon or fallback specified. The text and Fig. 1 claim an entropy bonus in the objective, but Eq. (3) contains none, and the supplement reports an entropy coefficient only for IU-Xray.

The motivation for RER is not fully justified: high reference-policy entropy does not imply that a particular poor response is unlikely under the reference policy. Entropy measures distributional diffuseness rather than the sampled response's probability. Alternatives such as token likelihood, sequence surprisal, or uncertainty-quality interaction baselines are not compared.

The SOTA comparison mixes methods that the paper itself says use altered splits, truncation, or additional resources. IU-Xray random 7:1:2 splits can also vary substantially. Without controlled reimplementation on identical splits and preprocessing, the small numerical margins do not convincingly establish a new state of the art. Reproducibility is further weakened by the missing promised code URL and unspecified random subset/seed. Table S8 also reports an 'Average' AUC of 0.873, inconsistent with the displayed per-category values, whose unweighted mean is approximately 0.791.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution. The paper addresses a relevant problem: stabilizing reinforcement learning for clinically oriented vision-language generation without an additional critic or preference annotations.

REVA-PO combines two understandable mechanisms: response-level KL weighting using advantage and reference-policy entropy, and periodic rollback/re-anchoring to the best validation checkpoint. The method is clearly presented with equations, pseudocode, and useful visual explanations.

The experiments cover two established chest X-ray report-generation datasets. On MIMIC-CXR, the reported improvements extend beyond BLEU to CheXpert F1 and RadGraph F1, and the stage-wise and RL-component ablations show broadly consistent gains.

The supplementary material includes reward-choice analysis, compute and memory overhead, model-size and group-size studies, prompts, and many training hyperparameters. The reported overhead of response-weighted regularization is modest.
weaknesses: The evidence does not convincingly establish that the improvements are attributable to the proposed RL algorithm. The RL ablation is not a complete factorial comparison: constant-KL is evaluated with VAPR and no-VAPR is evaluated with RER, but a plain fixed-reference GRPO baseline and all four RER/VAPR combinations are absent. This makes interaction effects and the strength of the core baseline unclear.

All principal results appear to come from single runs, with no variability or statistical significance. Several claimed state-of-the-art gains are small, such as IU-Xray BLEU-4 increasing from 0.192 to 0.199, so seed variation could affect the conclusions. The stability curves likewise lack uncertainty bands or repeated-run collapse rates.

The IU-Xray comparison is potentially unfair or at least insufficiently qualified: both the merger and disease classifier are initialized using MIMIC-CXR training, giving the method substantial external medical supervision for IU-Xray. This conflicts with the presentation that the approach uses only the standard dataset resources and is not accounted for in the SOTA comparison.

Clinical validation is inadequate for the strength of the claims. Clinical metrics are reported only on MIMIC-CXR, there is no radiologist evaluation, no analysis of clinically dangerous errors or pathology subgroups, and only two qualitative examples are provided. Optimizing BLEU-4 and then reporting overlap-based metrics also raises metric-alignment concerns. The sign-consistency analysis with CheXpert does not establish that BLEU optimization preserves clinical correctness.

There are technical inconsistencies and unsupported interpretations. Equation 6 is described as an unbiased estimator of KL(pi_theta || pi_ref), although trajectories are sampled from pi_theta_old; without correction it is not generally unbiased after the policies diverge. High reference entropy also does not imply that the reference is unlikely to generate a particular poor response, undermining the stated rationale for the negative-advantage branch of RER. No safeguards are specified for zero reward standard deviation in Equation 2 or zero within-group entropy range in Equation 8.

The description of VAPR is internally inconsistent: the text says validation occurs after each epoch, whereas Algorithm 1 places evaluation inside the step loop. The objective is also said to contain an entropy bonus, but Equation 3 contains none, and the implementation reports an entropy coefficient only for IU-Xray. These discrepancies materially hinder reproducibility.

VAPR is closely related to validation-based checkpoint selection and periodic rollback, making its algorithmic novelty modest. Because the same validation set repeatedly selects and resets the training trajectory, the paper should also examine validation overfitting and compare against simpler early stopping, rollback, or moving-reference baselines.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed supplement: the abstract's code link is blank, exact data split identifiers and random seeds are absent, and important generation and evaluation settings such as sampling temperature, top-p, maximum report length, test-time decoding, and text preprocessing are not specified.

There are notable reporting errors. Table S8 lists an average classifier AUC of 0.873, while the arithmetic mean of the 14 displayed category AUCs is approximately 0.791. Such an unexplained discrepancy reduces confidence in the empirical reporting. Overall, the work has promising ideas, but the fairness, technical, and evidentiary concerns currently favor rejection.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and relevant Algorithms/General contribution: RER provides response-level KL control without a critic or preference data, while VAPR periodically re-anchors optimization to a validation-best policy. The combination is intuitive, lightweight, and potentially transferable beyond chest X-ray reporting.

The empirical results are strong and broad. REVA-PO is evaluated on both MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray and improves multiple linguistic and clinical-efficacy metrics, including CheXpert F1 and RadGraph F1, rather than optimizing BLEU-4 alone.

The ablations provide useful evidence for the proposed components. Comparisons against constant KL, no KL, and no VAPR support the claims about sample efficiency and collapse prevention, while training curves expose the relevant dynamics rather than reporting only final scores.

The supplementary analysis substantially strengthens the work: it examines alternative rewards, reward-signal agreement, computational overhead, group size, model size, classifier performance, prompts, and detailed hyperparameters. The reported overhead of RER is modest.

The three-stage pipeline is practically motivated. Leveraging a pretrained LVLM and frozen disease classifier avoids specialized contrastive pretraining, and the method achieves competitive results using fewer auxiliary annotations than several prior systems.
The manuscript is generally well organized, technically accessible, and visually clear. It also candidly discusses failure modes of CheXpert F1 and RadGraph F1 as RL rewards.
weaknesses: The evaluation reports no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Because the headline gains over the strongest baselines are sometimes small and RL training is stochastic, it is unclear how much of the improvement exceeds run-to-run variance.

The baseline comparison does not fully isolate the algorithmic contribution. Table 4 lacks a clean vanilla-GRPO configuration with both constant KL and a fixed reference, as well as a complete 2x2 RER-by-VAPR ablation. Consequently, interaction effects and improvement over the direct optimization baseline remain somewhat ambiguous.

The claimed state-of-the-art comparison aggregates numbers from papers with heterogeneous preprocessing, data filtering, and potentially different IU-Xray splits. The supplement acknowledges some protocol differences, but reproducing representative strong baselines under one common pipeline would make the ranking more convincing.

Clinical evidence remains limited to automated labeler-based metrics and two qualitative examples. No radiologist evaluation, clinically stratified error analysis, or external-dataset validation is provided, so claims of superior clinical accuracy and practical reliability should be qualified.

Several technical and reproducibility details are inconsistent or underspecified. The text says validation occurs after each epoch, whereas Algorithm 1 places validation inside the step loop; an entropy bonus is mentioned in the overview and implementation details but is absent from Eq. 3; and the equations do not state how zero reward standard deviation or equal within-group entropies are handled.
There is at least one apparent reporting error: the 14 per-category AUC values in Table S8 average to approximately 0.791, not the reported 0.873. The manuscript should audit its numerical summaries.

RER's interpretation of reference entropy is heuristic: high distributional entropy does not necessarily imply that the reference assigns low probability to the particular sampled response. The paper demonstrates empirical effectiveness but offers limited theoretical justification or comparison with simpler response-level schedules.

Reproducibility is weakened by the blank public-code link, the unspecified seed and selection procedure for the 10,000-example RL subset, and the absence of training variance. These are mostly correctable but important given the substantial compute required.
